findings.title: Decoupling is explained as travel time: 'current bursts have to travel the whole loop, so a far cap can't deliver them in time', and the beads move at one fixed speed so longer loops take longer to go round
findings.problem: The QFN bench's main reliability lesson (boards 1–3: a bypass cap only helps when its loop to the chip's supply/ground pins is short) gives the wrong physical cause. When a loop is longer than max, the note in src/stations/qfn/logic.ts:274 reads: "Current bursts have to travel the whole loop, so a far cap can't deliver them in time." The CHECK visual makes the same claim. In src/stations/qfn/station.ts:228-230 each loop gets 5 beads with speed `.55/len`, a constant linear speed of about 0.55 m/s along the path, and the comment says "a long loop takes visibly longer". The player watches dots crawl round a 10-cell loop more slowly than round a 4-cell loop (shots qfn-teach-05, -08) and concludes that charge has to *travel* from the cap and arrives late. That is the 'current flows out to the device' / 'current arrives part by part' misconception DR-30 forbids. In reality the signal crosses a few cm of copper in well under a nanosecond. A far cap is worse because the longer loop encloses more area, so it has more **loop inductance**. Inductance resists a fast change in current (V = L·di/dt), so the voltage at the chip's pins sags (droops) before the cap's current can ramp up. Vendor and EDA guidance agrees that the mounting path's inductance dominates and limits the cap (https://www.ema-eda.com/ema-resources/blog/investigating-loop-inductance-understanding-impacts-and-optimization-strategies/, https://resources.pcb.cadence.com/blog/km-why-pdn-failures-rarely-come-from-too-few-capacitors). The beads also run on boards that are not powered or not complete: in qfn-teach-15 they run on C1's loop while GND is '4/6 pads' and the board 'Doesn't work' (DR-29). The mechanic itself, loop length measured on real copper, is right (logic.ts:264-274). Only the story and the visual are wrong, but the story is exactly the sentence a learner will remember.
findings.fix: 1) Note text in logic.ts:274. Replace it with: `${cap}'s loop to ${pair} is ${loop} cells (≤ ${max} wanted). A longer loop has more inductance: when the chip suddenly draws current, the voltage at its pins sags before the cap's current can ramp up.` 2) Visual in station.ts drawLoops/update. Light the whole loop at once: all beads start together and are evenly spaced round the loop, so u is offset by k/5, not by -k*.09. Use ONE speed for every loop, so a long loop isn't slower; a long loop just has more beads. Show the consequence at the chip instead: add a small supply 'droop' needle or status LED on the U1 body. Droop ∝ loop length (for example droop% = 3·loop). Over 12 % (loop > 4), the LED flickers and the chip 'blinks' (a reset), and the too-long loop's segments flash. 3) Only run the bursts when the chip's supply nets are joined (`r.nets` VDD/VIN and GND done). Otherwise show nothing. 4) Rename the panel row 'Loop C1' to 'C1 loop (shorter = less sag)'.
findings.verify: Unit test in src/stations/qfn/logic.test.ts: the far-cap note matches /inductance/ and not /travel|in time/. Retake qfn-teach-05 and -08 after CHECK at +0.3 s and +1.0 s: beads are evenly spaced round the whole loop at once; the 10-cell loop shows the chip LED flickering, the 4-cell loop a steady LED. Retake qfn-teach-15: no beads while GND isn't joined.
findings.verify_reason: Confirmed in both code and screenshots. logic.ts:274 has the 'travel the whole loop … deliver them in time' note; my logic check returned that exact string for C1 at [2,7] (loop 10). station.ts:230 gives each loop 5 beads at u=-k*.09 with speed .55/len. That is a constant linear speed, and the beads enter one after another from the cap, so they both 'arrive part by part' and go round a long loop more slowly (DR-30). qfn-teach-05 and -08 show this. The loop-inductance explanation in the fix is the standard correct one. One cited example is weak: in qfn-teach-15 the chip IS supplied from J1 (VIN joined, and the GND track J1.2–U1.2 is laid; only J2.2 and R1.2 are open), so that shot is not an unpowered loop. I reproduced a real DR-29 case instead: reference placement, only C1↔U1 copper, J1 unwired, VDD 2/3, GND 2/3, 'Doesn't work'. On CHECK the beads still run round C1's loop and the panel shows 'Loop C1 4 cells · ≤ 4' in green.

findings.title: Thermal vias cool the chip to 70 °C even when nothing is on layer 2 for them to carry heat into; in the reference route 3 of the 4 thermal vias end in bare laminate
findings.problem: Board 3's heat lesson is 'thermal vias carry the chip's heat into the other copper' (logic.ts:94, note at :278: 'every via is one more path into layer 2'). The check doesn't model the other copper at all. logic.ts:276-277 counts every via whose cell lies in the EP and puts it into T = 25 + P/(1/110 + n/300), whatever is on layer 2. In my run (qfn-teach-21-win, qfn-teach-19-b3-vias-4) the only layer-2 track had failed, so layer 2 held a single 2-cell GND stub far from the chip. Four EP vias still took the chip from 135 to 70 °C, green, 'reliable' on heat. Even the hand-made REFERENCE.driver (logic.ts:316-317) has EP vias at [6,3], [6,4] and [6,5] that touch no layer-2 copper: the layer-2 GND track starts at [7,4]. So three of the four 'heat paths' end in nothing. A via moves heat only to the copper it lands on, and the copper area on the far side sets the limit. With too little receiving copper, more vias add little (https://www.lcsc.com/blog/qfn-pcb-layout-guide/, ROHM https://fscdn.rohm.com/en/products/databook/applinote/ic/common/heat_dissipation_effect_of_thermal_via_in_exposed_pad_type_package_an-e.pdf, Pericom https://www.pericom.com/assets/App-Note-Files/TQFN-Package-thermal-via-design-guide.pdf). As built, the game teaches 'more holes under the chip = cooler', which is the rule of thumb a beginner gets wrong in a real layout. The concept isn't the mechanic: the player only counts to 4.
findings.fix: In check() (logic.ts:276-278), count a thermal via only if its layer-2 node sits in a layer-2 GND copper component of at least K cells, and let that component's size set the spreading term. Example: T = ambient + P / (1/θ_board + 1/(θ_via/n + θ_spread)), with θ_spread = 900/cellsL2, where cellsL2 is the number of layer-2 GND cells (tracks, vias, through-hole pads) in the components the EP vias reach. To keep the lesson playable without a new tool, put an automatic layer-2 GND pour under the EP footprint (the 9 EP cells) as soon as the first EP via goes in. Draw it on layer 2 in station.ts redraw (a soft GND-blue square under the chip, visible when LAYER L2 is on). The player then makes it bigger by running layer-2 GND copper out from it. Retune P/θ so the reference still needs exactly 4 vias, and update REFERENCE.driver so every EP via joins the pour. Note text: 'Vias carry heat to copper on layer 2. With little copper there, they have nowhere to put it.' Update logic.test.ts:70-80, which expects {vias:3,temp:77}.
findings.verify: New unit test: driver REFERENCE with every layer-2 trace removed has thermal.temp > limit even with 4 EP vias. With the reference layer-2 copper restored it is ≤ limit. Retake qfn-teach-32 with LAYER L2: the pour under the EP is visible and joined to the GND track.
findings.verify_reason: Confirmed in code and by a logic run. logic.ts:276-277 counts every via inside the EP cells and ignores layer-2 copper. I ran check() on REFERENCE.driver with all layer-2 traces removed: thermal={vias:4,temp:70,limit:70}, still green on heat. In the reference, only the via at [7,4] (and [10,2], outside the EP) touches a layer-2 trace; [6,4], [6,3] and [6,5] touch none. The claim is real. Lowered to P2 because the parallel-heat-path idea is correct at the level taught, and in normal play the layer-2 GND route reaches at least one EP via. What's missing is the spreading-copper term, which is a refinement, not a reversal. Note also that qfn-teach-21-win is not a win: it is a send-back (GND 4/6, 'Sent back from test'), because in run1 the layer-2 trace starting at [7,4] was attempted before that EP via existed.
extra_evidence: mockups/review5/tools/verify-qfn-teach/v1.mjs output: f1 thermal {vias:4,temp:70} with no layer-2 traces; f1l2 shows [6,4],[6,3],[6,5] with l2:false

findings.title: The board-3 chip glows red-hot at 135 °C the moment the board loads, before anything powers it
findings.problem: Board 3 drops in with U1 tinted orange-red, a pulsing red glow sprite and the panel row 'Chip 135 °C · ≤ 70', before a single track exists (qfn-teach-13-b3-start-chip-hot-unpowered). The run log at that moment reads thermal {vias:0,temp:135}, with VIN at 1/4 pads and GND at 1/6. chipTemp() (logic.ts:233) depends only on the via count. update() (station.ts:393-396) tints and pulses the body from it whether or not the chip has VIN and GND. The tint stays in every later shot, including while GND is still open (qfn-teach-15). The cause and effect is backwards: a chip heats because current flows through it once it is powered. Showing a disconnected chip at 135 °C teaches that heat belongs to the part, or to the vias, rather than to the power it dissipates. It also gives the answer away (the red chip says 'put vias here') before the player has wired anything. That cuts against DR-37 (the world shows the rule) and DR-28 (failure shown as a consequence of the player's design).
findings.fix: In check(), compute `powered` = nets VIN and GND both done (or at least U1.1, U1.2 and U1.EP joined to J1). While unpowered, set thermal = {vias:n,temp:HEAT.ambient,limit,powered:false}. Don't push the thermal note or mark the board unreliable for heat; the board is tier 0 anyway because nets are open. In station.ts:393-396, ramp the tint and glow only when thermal.powered. Lerp it over about 1.5 s so the player sees the chip *warm up* the moment the last supply track lands, which is the payoff beat. Panel row (station.ts:417): show 'Chip — (no power)' until powered.
findings.verify: Retake qfn-teach-13: the chip body is its normal ink colour and the panel shows 'Chip — (no power)'. Then lay the layer-1 VIN/GND tracks and capture at +0.2 s and +1.5 s: the chip warms to orange. Unit test: blank(driver) gives thermal.temp === 25.
findings.verify_reason: Confirmed. check(blank(driver)) returns thermal {vias:0,temp:135,limit:70}, because chipTemp depends only on the via count (logic.ts:233, 277). station.ts:393-396 tints and pulses the body with no power check. qfn-teach-13 shows a red-hot U1 with VIN 1/4 and GND 1/6. The finding has DR-37 backwards, though: DR-37 asks the world to show hidden rules BEFORE the player can fail them, so an early hot chip partly satisfies it. Lowered to P2: the misread (heat belongs to the part) lasts only until the first VIN/GND tracks go in, and the via→cooling cause and effect still reads. The fix keeps the foreshadowing, since layer-1 supply tracks are laid before vias, so the chip still warms before the player drops vias. The cited qfn-teach-15 is a powered state (VIN joined and J1→U1 GND laid), so it is not evidence of 'tint while unpowered'.
extra_evidence: v1.mjs output f2: {vias:0,temp:135,limit:70} on a blank board 3
mockups/review5/shots/qfn-teach-13-b3-start-chip-hot-unpowered.jpg
findings.fix_correction: Gate on U1.1 (VIN), U1.2 (GND) and J1's pins being on one piece of copper, not on the whole VIN/GND nets being done. Otherwise the chip stays cold until J2 and R1 are wired, which is too late to foreshadow the heat.

findings.title: Shipping a 'Works' (unreliable) board has no consequence: the decoupling and heat lessons are only a grade word and a toast, never an event
findings.problem: I shipped board 1 with C1 down by the connector (loop 10 cells, tier 1) and the toast read 'Shipped · Works. Placement comes before routing…' (qfn-teach-09-b1-ship-tier1). That teach line is about placement, not the flaw that was just shipped. Nothing in the world reacts: the board slides into the stack, the next board drops in, and the crew cheers (station.ts:284-287 always plays cheer() and a.cheer() for tier ≥ 1). The same holds for board 3 at 77 °C (qfn-teach-33, -34): a 'Works' board can be shipped and is just a lower tier. Only tier 0 has a failure moment (send-back with groan, alarm and red rings, station.ts:283; qfn-teach-02, -21). So the two physical concepts of this room, supply droop and heat, never *fail* in front of the player. They are numbers to push into the green ('10 cells · ≤ 4', '77 °C · ≤ 70'), which is learning the panel rather than the physics. Review 4 proposed a physical payoff (carry the tray to the reflow oven, tombstoning, a test that shows the droop) and it is still NOT BUILT. The room's reflow oven, pick-and-place and inspection box (room.ts:29-48) are scenery that the job never touches.
findings.fix: Add a 2–3 s 'bring-up test' on SHIP for tier ≥ 1, staged on the board itself or on the inspection box at (7.6, -6.8) (room.ts:46). Give each board a small status LED part. Decoupling loop over max: on power-up the LED stutters, the chip shows a 'reset' blink, the too-long loop flashes orange, and the toast says 'Works, but the MCU resets when it gets busy: C2's loop is too long.' Thermal over limit: the chip glows, a small heat-shimmer or smoke puff rises, and the LED blinks slowly (thermal throttling). Tier 2/3: steady LED, then the cheer. Play cheer() only for tier ≥ 2 and a softer 'meh' chime for tier 1. Keep it never-a-fail (still shipped, no mistake), per DR-02. Optional room tie-in: SHIP puts the board on the reflow-oven conveyor, and the board comes out the far end where the inspection monitor shows the LED test.
findings.verify: Ship board 1 with C1 at [2,7] (the qfn-teach run1 script) and capture at +0.5 s and +1.5 s after SHIP: the LED stutters and the loop flashes. Board 3 with 3 vias: smoke or shimmer at the chip. Spec: tests/station-qfn.spec.ts still reaches won with tier-1 boards and mistakes stays 0.
findings.verify_reason: Confirmed in code and screenshots. station.ts:284-286 always plays a.cheer() and cheer() for tier ≥ 1, then shows b.teach. That is the board's fixed teach line (logic.ts:80), not the flaw just shipped. qfn-teach-09 shows the 'Shipped · Works. Placement comes before routing…' toast after shipping a 10-cell loop. Only tier 0 has a failure beat (station.ts:283). The oven and AOI (room.ts:39-48) are scenery. The review-4 payoff (DESIGN_A.md:85-87) is not built. The fix keeps the never-a-fail rule (DR-02).

findings.title: Board 1's lesson ('the order of the pins around the chip decides where the connector can go') never happens: the header routes from any edge
findings.problem: Board 1's teach line (logic.ts:80), shown on ship, says placement decides routability through pin order. But a header can only be rotated, never mirrored, and rotation keeps its cyclic pin order (VDD → GND → SIG). That order always matches the chip's counter-clockwise order VDD(1) → GND(2) → OUT(9). So on one layer *every* edge placement with the mouth out is routable. I proved it in-game: J1 on the RIGHT edge ([12,4], rot 2) instead of the reference's bottom edge routes cleanly to 'Works reliably' (qfn-teach-30; log: tier 2, cost 43, no problems). Placement only changes track length (par). The player cannot experience the stated rule, so the line reads as a claim to memorise, not a lesson learned by doing. A player can solve board 1 by trial and error (drop J1 on any edge, then trace around) without ever thinking about pin order. Board 1 also loads four new ideas at once: one layer, connector orientation, series resistor and a hidden decoupling loop (logic.ts:84 `decouple` with nothing in the ask). That breaks DR-27's one-new-idea step.
findings.fix: Make pin order a real decision. Put two headers in the crate for board 1: J1a (VDD, GND, SIG) and J1b (SIG, GND, VDD, the mirrored pinout of a different cable), with only one on the board's BOM. A player who picks the wrong one finds that no edge routes without a crossing. Swap in the PartDef via a new 'swap' act on a click of the spare in the crate tray. Alternatively, lock J1 to an enclosure slot (locked:true, like J1/J2 on board 3) and make the chip's pin order the thing to read. At minimum, rewrite the teach text to what the board actually teaches: 'On one layer, tracks can't cross: the net nearest the chip stays on the inside all the way to the connector.' Move decoupling off board 1 (drop `decouple` from sensor, logic.ts:84), or name it in the ask, so board 2 introduces it cleanly.
findings.verify: Unit test: with the mirrored header (J1b) on any edge and rotation, an exhaustive search over edge placements finds no legal one-layer routing (or at least the reference and the right-edge route both fail traceProblem with a short). With J1a, both succeed. Retake qfn-teach-30 with J1b: CHECK reports a short or open net.
findings.verify_reason: Confirmed in code and by a logic run. In check(), J1 at [12,4] rot 2 with the right-edge routing gives tier 2, no problems, cost 43 (it routes cleanly, but not under par 22). It works because rotation keeps the header's handedness and the board outside the chip is a ring, so any edge with the mouth out is topologically equivalent. Placement changes only length and par. The teach line (logic.ts:80) is therefore not something the player can experience. The sensor board also carries decouple (logic.ts:84), which its ask never mentions, so board 1 marks a far cap 'Works' for a concept board 2 introduces (DR-27). P1 is fair given both issues.
extra_evidence: v1.mjs output f4: {tier:2,problems:[],cost:43} for J1 on the right edge

findings.title: Asks, the job card and a wall poster print the method ('two caps hug their pins', 'Use layer 2 and vias', 'cap beside the pins'), so the decoupling and layer-2 ideas are read, not discovered
findings.problem: The places that tell the player the answer: (a) Board 2's ask (logic.ts:86, shown in the bench panel at station.ts:416; shot qfn-teach-09): 'Each needs its own 100 nF cap hugging its VDD and GND pins.' (b) The job-card step (station.ts:73; card in qfn-teach-09): 'Board 2 · Decoupling: two caps hug their pins'. (c) A wall poster in the room (room.ts:60-61): 'SHORT LOOP / cap beside the pins (not across the board)'. (d) Board 3's ask (logic.ts:93): 'Use layer 2 and vias, and cool the exposed pad', and its card 'layer 2, vias, thermal pad'. Together they print the solution before the player meets the problem, so the board becomes 'follow the instruction', not 'apply the idea'. DR-39 wants goals to say *what* (an object and an outcome), not *how*. With the failure consequence missing (see the 'Works' finding above), reading the ask is the only way the player learns why caps go near pins. The teach line after shipping (logic.ts:87) is well worded and truthful ('supplies brief bursts of current (it is not a battery)'), but it repeats what the ask already said.
findings.fix: State the need, not the method. Board 2 ask: 'This MCU resets whenever its supply sags. Wire it so it stays up.' Card: 'Board 2 · Decoupling: keep the MCU from resetting'. Board 3 ask: 'Power passes through to J2, whose pins are flipped. Route it, and keep the LED driver under its temperature.' Card: 'Board 3 · Two layers: cross VIN and GND, keep it cool'. Keep the LAYER/VIA buttons lighting up on board 3 as the world's hint. Move the 'SHORT LOOP' poster's method line into the post-ship teach toast, or change the poster to a picture only (two loops, a small one and a big one, with a sad and a happy chip face) so it hints without the sentence. Pair this with the bring-up test so failure teaches the method.
findings.verify: Read every BOARDS[].ask and job.steps[].text: no 'hug', 'beside', 'use layer 2', 'vias'. Retake the qfn-teach-09 and -13 bench shots and count the words in the panel ask.
findings.verify_reason: The strings are as cited: logic.ts:86 ('hugging its VDD and GND pins'), logic.ts:93 ('Use layer 2 and vias'), station.ts:73 card steps ('two caps hug their pins', 'layer 2, vias, thermal pad'), room.ts:60-61 poster. The card steps do name the method and tool, which breaks DR-39. Lowered to P2 for two reasons. The bench ask sits on the station's own panel, which is the place DR-40/DR-49 allow text. And until the consequence from finding 3 exists, stripping the method would leave board 2 under-explained. The card wording is the cheap, clear part. A poster is allowed signage, though a picture-only version is nicer.
extra_evidence: mockups/review5/shots/qfn-teach-09-b1-ship-tier1.jpg (card 'Board 2 · Decoupling: two caps hug their pins' and the panel ask)
findings.fix_correction: Do the card text now. Change the bench asks only together with finding 3's bring-up test, so the failure teaches the method before the hint is removed.

findings.title: 'Too long' (orange) and 'short enough' (green) decoupling loops look the same on the copper, and the failing panel row isn't red
findings.problem: drawLoops (station.ts:223) draws each loop with an *additive* glow, '#7dffb0' (ok) or '#ffa040' (too long), at ×1.4, opacity .55, over copper that is already saturated red (VDD/VIN) and blue (GND). Additive colour on red or blue washes to pale cream, peach or lavender either way. In the crops, the 10-cell too-long loop (qfn-teach-05-loopcrop) is a peach stripe on red and lilac on blue; the 4-cell good loop (qfn-teach-30-loopcrop) is a cream stripe on red and pale cyan on blue. Without reading the panel, a first-time player can't tell which loop is bad. The beads are near-white in both states too (hot('#c8ffe0'|'#ffd0a0',2), station.ts:230). The panel doesn't help: a failing loop row uses class 'no', which styles the value in neutral ink-2 (src/ui/ui.css:225), so '10 cells · ≤ 4' looks like a normal stat (qfn-teach-07-b1-farcap-panel). Meanwhile 'Track + vias 22 · par 22' is also neutral, because the row is keyed on tier===3 (station.ts:418), not on cost ≤ par. On that board the cost *was* at par, so a met target looks unmet. The device-shows-its-state rule (DR-47) fails for the station's key visual.
findings.fix: Draw the loop as a normal-blended (not additive) outline *beside* the copper. Use two thin parallel strips offset ±0.045 from the track centreline, with an ink edge (outline on). Solid green #2fbf71 when ok; when too long, orange #ff7a1a with a slow 2 Hz pulse and a dashed pattern. Draw a small sad or happy face icon at the cap. Panel: give failing reliability rows class 'bad' (red, ui.css:225 already defines li.bad) instead of 'no'. Compute the par row's ok as `r.cost<=r.par`, independent of tier.
findings.verify: Retake qfn-teach-05 and qfn-teach-30 crops. In greyscale and in colour, the too-long loop reads orange or dashed and the good loop green or solid. Measure ΔE between the two loop strips: > 40. Panel crop: '10 cells · ≤ 4' renders red, '22 · par 22' green.
findings.verify_reason: Confirmed. station.ts:223 uses additive blending (#7dffb0 vs #ffa040 ×1.4, opacity .55). In the crops, the 10-cell bad loop reads peach/lavender and the 4-cell good loop cream/pale cyan, which are hard to tell apart (qfn-teach-05-loopcrop vs qfn-teach-30-loopcrop). The beads are near-white in both states (station.ts:230). The panel's failing loop row uses class 'no', which ui.css:225 renders in neutral ink-2, and the par row is keyed on tier===3 (station.ts:418). In qfn-teach-05 '22 · par 22' is at par but shows neutral. Without reading, the player can't tell which loop is bad (AGENTS 2, DR-47).

findings.title: The chip limit of 70 °C teaches a wrong rule of thumb: a chip at 77 °C is marked unreliable, though 70 °C is a commercial *ambient* range and silicon junctions run to 125–150 °C
findings.problem: HEAT = {power:1, ambient:25, board:110, via:300, limit:70} (logic.ts:232). The note says 'The chip runs at 77 °C (it must stay at or under 70 °C)' (qfn-teach-33/-34). A learner takes away '70 °C is too hot for a chip'. Datasheets pair a 0–70 °C *commercial ambient* range with a 125 °C junction limit, and silicon is often limited to 150 °C (Allegro AN295014, https://www.allegromicro.com/-/media/files/application-notes/an295014-computing-ic-temperature-rise.pdf; ICS datasheets via alldatasheet). Mixing up ambient and junction ratings is a classic beginner mistake, and the game teaches it. The per-via figure (300 °C/W) is in a plausible range: one vendor estimate is about 176 °C/W for a 0.3 mm via in 1.6 mm board (https://www.bestpcbs.com/blog/2026/07/thermal-vias/). Only the limit is off.
findings.fix: Use HEAT = {power:1.6, ambient:25, board:110, via:300, limit:100}, and label the row and note as the *chip* (junction), with a reason: 'must stay ≤ 100 °C for a long life (its absolute max is 125 °C)'. This keeps viasNeeded() = 4 and the reference unchanged: chipTemp(3) = 108.8 °C > 100 and chipTemp(4) = 96.4 °C ≤ 100, and 0 vias gives 201 °C, a dramatic start. Update logic.test.ts:73 ({vias:3,temp:109,limit:100}) and :79.

findings.title: 'Elegant to manufacture' and 'Shorter routes … are cheaper to make' name the wrong cost driver
findings.problem: Tier 3 is named 'Elegant to manufacture' (station.ts:26). The tier-2 note says 'Track + vias cost N; par is P. Shorter routes and fewer vias are cheaper to make.' (logic.ts:282; shot qfn-teach-30). Copper track length is not a fabrication cost driver: fabs price on board area, layer count, hole count and size, and minimum feature sizes (https://www.protoexpress.com/kb/pcb-price-composition/, https://jlcpcb.com/blog/breaking-down-pcb-pricing-how-is-the-cost-determined). The via half is right: drill hits do cost. Tying par to 'cheaper' teaches that long tracks cost money, rather than the real reasons short tracks are better (less resistance, inductance and coupling; easier to inspect).
findings.fix: Rename tier 3 'Elegant' (TIERS[3]) and bonus text 'Elegant: every route at or under par' (keep it). Change the note to: 'Track + vias: N; par is P. Shorter tracks have less resistance and pick up less noise, and every via is another hole to drill.' Keep VIA_COST = 2 and its comment, which is truthful.
findings.verify: grep -n 'cheaper to make\|to manufacture' src/stations/qfn returns nothing. Retake the toast crop from qfn-teach-30.
findings.verify_reason: TIERS[3]='Elegant to manufacture' (station.ts:26). The tier-2 note at logic.ts:282 says 'Shorter routes and fewer vias are cheaper to make'; it appears in qfn-teach-30's toast. Track length is not a fab cost driver. The via half is fine (VIA_COST comment at logic.ts:19).
extra_evidence: mockups/review5/shots/qfn-teach-30-b1-connector-right-edge-reliable.jpg (toast text)

findings.title: Notes refer to 'U1 pin 1/U1 pin 2' and 'U1 pin 8/U1 pin 7', but the chip shows only net names, never pin numbers
findings.problem: The decoupling notes build pin references as `${part} pin ${n}` (logic.ts:273-274), e.g. 'C1's loop to U1 pin 1/U1 pin 2 is 10 cells' (qfn-teach-05 toast) and 'No bypass cap is wired to U1 pin 1 and U1 pin 2'. The QFN model prints only each used pin's net name (VDD, GND, OUT) beside its pad (station.ts:156-159), plus the pin-1 dot (station.ts:151). On board 2 the MCU has two VDD and two GND pins (logic.ts:88), so a note about 'U1 pin 8/U1 pin 7' can't be matched to the right-hand pair without counting pins from the dot, a skill the game never teaches. The reader is pushed to the text when the world should carry the meaning (DR-47, DR-50).
findings.fix: Either (a) print a small pin number in the tag (label(`${n} ${pin.label}`) at station.ts:158), which also teaches the counter-clockwise numbering the poster hints at (room.ts:58-59); or (b) phrase the notes by side, with a helper `side(ref)` → 'left'/'right'/'top'/'bottom' from QFN_PINS: "C2's loop to the right-hand VDD/GND pins is 6 cells". Also pulse the pads of the failing pair on CHECK (reuse showMarks rings at station.ts:240-244 for loops over max).
findings.verify: Board 2 with C2 far (logic.test.ts:54-63 layout): the CHECK toast names a side, or pins whose numbers are visible in the bench crop, and rings pulse on pins 7/8.
findings.verify_reason: logic.ts:273 builds 'U1 pin 1/U1 pin 2'; qfn-teach-05's toast shows it. The QFN model prints only net-name tags beside used pins (station.ts:156-159) and a pin-1 dot (station.ts:151). Pin numbers appear nowhere, so 'U1 pin 8/U1 pin 7' on board 2 can't be matched without counting.
extra_evidence: mockups/review5/shots/qfn-teach-05-b1-farcap-check-beads.jpg (chip tags read VDD/GND/OUT; toast says 'U1 pin 1/U1 pin 2')

findings.title: The exposed pad is 'not connected' on boards 1–2 and refuses copper; real QFN EPs are soldered down and usually tied to GND
findings.problem: The temp sensor and the MCU are defined with EP 'NC' (logic.ts:81, :88), printed on the body as 'EP: not connected' (station.ts:153; visible in qfn-teach-05). Any track into the EP is refused: 'That is U1 pin EP (NC). Copper there would join it to …' (logic.ts:159). Real datasheets vary, but common guidance is to solder the EP down and tie it to ground. Some parts allow floating, and it must never go to another potential (NXP EB806 https://NXP.com/docs/en/engineering-bulletin/EB806.pdf; TI E2E https://e2e.ti.com/support/interface-group/interface/f/interface-forum/118754/tusb2046b---exposed-thermal-pad-on-qfn-package-soldered-to-gnd-or-left-floating). Two of three boards teach 'the big centre pad is unconnected and must be avoided', which is the less common case. Separately, the via rule 'No via inside a small pad: solder would wick down it' (logic.ts:181) silently doesn't apply to the EP, though EP vias also wick solder and cause voiding, which is why they're kept small or plugged (https://www.lcsc.com/blog/qfn-pcb-layout-guide/). Review 4 noted the QFN package itself (solder underneath, EP as heat path) is barely taught; that is still true apart from the poster (room.ts:58-59).
findings.fix: Make the MCU's EP 'GND' (logic.ts:88), and add 'U1.EP' to the GND net there. The EP's solid pad then joins GND copper for free, which is also a nice routing shortcut that teaches 'the EP is a ground pad'. For the sensor, keep NC but label it 'EP: solder only (no net)'. In viaProblem's EP branch, add a soft note on the first EP via: 'Thermal vias are kept small (or plugged) so solder doesn't wick away from the pad.'
findings.verify: Unit tests: the mcu REFERENCE is still reliable at par (or re-par it), and routing GND through U1.EP is legal. Retake the board-2 bench shot: the chip reads 'EP: GND'.
findings.verify_reason: The code facts are as cited: EP 'NC' on the sensor and MCU (logic.ts:81, :88), the 'EP: not connected' print (station.ts:153), NC refusal (logic.ts:159), and the EP exempt from the small-pad wicking rule (logic.ts:181). An NC EP on a temp sensor is realistic, so that half is mild. An MCU EP is usually VSS/GND. The via-in-pad inconsistency was raised in review 4 (DESIGN_A.md:25, 'Reconcile the via-in-pad rule with QFN', :247) and is still unresolved, so this is a carry-over, not new.
extra_evidence: mockups/review4/DESIGN_A.md:25 and :247 (same via-in-pad contradiction, still open)
findings.fix_correction: If the MCU EP becomes GND, the U1.2→EP→U1.7 shortcut under the body makes board 2's GND trivially short. Re-par 'mcu' (currently 35) and recheck that REFERENCE.mcu still costs exactly par (logic.test.ts reference test).

findings.title: 'L2 · bottom, thin tracks' suggests the bottom layer has thinner copper by nature
findings.problem: The panel row 'Drawing on: L2 · bottom, thin tracks' (station.ts:417; qfn-teach-32) and the narrower layer-2 render width (.052 vs .07, station.ts:197) present thinner tracks as a property of layer 2. On a real two-layer board both outer layers are the same copper and either can carry wide or narrow tracks. The width is a design choice set by current and spacing. The thinner render is a readability device for seeing the two layers at once, which is fine, but the label states it as fact.
findings.fix: Change the row text to 'L2 · bottom (drawn thinner so both layers show)', or just 'L1 · top' / 'L2 · bottom'.
findings.verify: Retake qfn-teach-32 and read the panel row.
findings.verify_reason: station.ts:417 prints 'L2 · bottom, thin tracks' (and 'L1 · top, wide tracks'). station.ts:197 draws layer 2 at .052 vs .07 width. Track width is a design choice, not a layer property. This is a minor wording issue.
extra_evidence: mockups/review5/shots/qfn-teach-15-b3-no-thermal-check.jpg (panel 'L1 · top, wide tracks')

findings.title: Board 3 is an 'LED driver' with no LED, and every passive's purpose (ISET resistor, RST pull-up, series R) is invisible: the parts are just two-pad blocks
findings.problem: Board 3's U1 is an 'LED driver' with VIN, GND and ISET (logic.ts:95), but it has no LED output pin, no LED part and no output connector. J2 is just 'power out' passing VIN/GND through. R1 (2 kΩ, ISET to GND) supposedly sets LED current that never flows. On board 2, R1 10 kΩ VDD→RST is a reset pull-up; on board 1, R1 100 Ω is a series output resistor. None of these purposes is ever shown or used: the values aren't drawn on the parts (twoPin tags show only the id, station.ts:174), and nothing depends on the value. The QFN bench is about layout, so this is acceptable scope. But a chip named 'LED driver' with nothing to drive invites the confusion 'what does this do?' and misses a cheap moment of meaning.
findings.fix: Make J2 'LED out' (pins LED+ and LED−/GND), with U1 pin 9 renamed OUT and ISET moved to pin 10, or keep the pass-through and rename U1 'regulator' with R1 as a feedback/enable resistor. Draw each passive's value on its body plate (label `${p.id} ${p.value}`). On the bring-up test (see the 'Works' finding), light a small LED strip on J2 when board 3 passes, so the board visibly does its job.
findings.verify: Retake the board-3 bench shot: the parts show values, and SHIP lights the LED on the output.
findings.verify_reason: U1 'LED driver' has VIN, GND and ISET only (logic.ts:95). J2 is 'power out' passing VIN/GND. There is no LED part or LED output. Passive tags show only the id (station.ts:174: label(p.id,…)); values never appear on the parts. This is acceptable scope for a layout bench, so P2.

findings.title: While dropping thermal vias, the chip turns into a pink see-through wash under a pulsing glow; once dropped, the vias are hidden under the opaque body
findings.problem: With VIA armed or LAYER 2 on, the QFN body goes to opacity .28 (station.ts:216-217), and the over-limit heat sprite pulses on top of it at .35–.60 (station.ts:137, :396). In qfn-teach-18 the EP, where the player is meant to click, sits under a pink-orange bloom, and the 3×3 cells can't be told apart. That is the 'part being taught' DR-66 says glow must never hide, and the peak .6 is above the ≤ 0.5 cap. Once VIA is disarmed, the body is opaque again and the four thermal vias the player just placed can't be seen at all (qfn-teach-19-b3-vias-4, qfn-teach-21-win). The only evidence of the heat lesson is then the panel number.
findings.fix: Cap the heat sprite's opacity at .45 and shrink it to .6, offset above the body edge, not over the EP. While VIA is armed, draw the EP's 9 cells as a crisp outlined grid on top (renderOrder 5, no glow) with the hover square. When disarmed on board 3, show the placed thermal vias as small dots printed on the body's top texture, the way real packages show nothing but a heat-cam would: 'n thermal vias' pips on the body edge.
findings.verify: Retake qfn-teach-18: all 9 EP cells are distinct and the hover square is visible. Retake qfn-teach-19-b3-vias-4: 4 pips or dots are visible on the chip.
findings.verify_reason: With VIA armed, the body goes to opacity .28 (station.ts:216-217) under a pulsing additive sprite. Its peak opacity is .35+.25=.60 (station.ts:396), above DR-66's 0.5. In qfn-teach-18 the chip area is a pink-orange wash. Once disarmed, the placed thermal vias are hidden under the opaque body (qfn-teach-19-b3-vias-4 shows none). The sprite is also glow(g,…,.9) (station.ts:137; kit.ts:66-69 sets scale=size), 0.9 wide over a 0.47-wide body, about 1.9× its source. That breaks DR-66's ≤1.5× rule too. The EP is drawn as one 3×3 box (station.ts:144), so its cells are never individually visible, glow or not.

src/stations/qfn/station.ts:144 (EP drawn as a single box, no cell grid)

findings.title: The 'teaching grid' disclosure is hidden unless the game is paused
findings.problem: The bench panel renders the stand-in disclosure 'Teaching grid: cell sizes and loop limits are this bench's rules. A real layout still needs the fab's DRC and an electrical review.' (station.ts:419). But `.station-panel .profile{display:none}` is shown only under body[data-paused] (src/ui/ui.css:226-228), so it never appears during play (none of the bench shots show it). DR-32 asks that stand-ins be labelled. The 4-cell loop limit and the cell grid are exactly the numbers a learner might carry into real work.
findings.fix: Put a short always-on stand-in tag on the board's near margin plate, next to the legend (station.ts:110-111): 'teaching grid · not to scale', ≤ 5 words. Keep the full sentence for pause.
findings.verify: Retake the board-1 bench shot: the margin shows 'teaching grid · not to scale'.

This is a deliberate choice, though: the comment at ui.css:227 says caveats show when paused, not mid-play, which trades DR-32 against DR-40. A ≤5-word always-on margin tag satisfies both.

notes.teaching: The QFN bench is still the strongest 'concept is the mechanic' station, and most of its logic holds up. One copper layer really can't cross, and the pen refuses with a reason (shorts are prevented at the gesture, not graded later). Connectivity is a real breadth-first search over copper. The decoupling loop is measured on the actual copper path from cap to the chip's pin pair. Vias really change layer. The thermal model is a correct parallel-conductance formula with visible diminishing returns: 135 → 105 → 88 → 77 → 70 °C for 0 to 4 vias, from the run log. The lesson breaks in four places. (1) The *why* of decoupling is wrong: the note and the constant-speed beads teach 'current takes time to travel', not 'loop inductance makes the supply sag' (logic.ts:274, station.ts:228-230). (2) Thermal vias work even when they land on nothing on layer 2. Three of the four vias in the hand-made reference land on bare laminate, and my broken run still reached 70 °C. (3) The chip is red-hot before it is powered. (4) Board 1's stated lesson (pin order decides connector placement) can't be experienced: the header routes from any edge (qfn-teach-30). Because shipping a tier-1 board has no consequence, reliability is learned as 'push the panel numbers into the green'. A player can succeed by trial and error: move C1 until the loop row says ≤ 4, add vias until the chip row turns green. That is still doing, not reading, but the understanding sits in the toast text. The numbers to retune: a 70 °C chip limit teaches an ambient rating as a junction rating; use 1.6 W and 100 °C, which keeps 4 vias. 'Cheaper to make' for shorter tracks names the wrong cost driver. CHECK is free and only a tier-0 SHIP counts as a mistake, which is good (DR-02).
notes.clarity: The bench framing, keycaps, dashed ratsnest and live net checklist read well, and the modeless input fixed in review 4 holds (5 buttons: TURN, LAYER, VIA, CHECK, SHIP). Clarity problems that hurt the lesson: the ok and too-long loop glows both wash to pale stripes over red and blue copper (additive blend), and a failing loop row renders in neutral ink, not red. Notes cite 'U1 pin 8/pin 7' but the chip shows no pin numbers. Asks, the job card and the SHORT LOOP poster print the method ('caps hug their pins', 'use layer 2 and vias'). The send-back cue (rings on every unjoined pad) doesn't point at the part the toast names (J1's mouth). The thermal vias become invisible once placed. The panel's ask plus rows is about 40 words, which is within the bench-monitor allowance but long.
notes.fun: Routing still plays like a satisfying Flow-Free puzzle. Pads chime when a net joins, parts drop in with a clatter, the send-back groans with the crew alarm, and par invites a replay. The room around it (reflow oven, pick-and-place, inspection box) is scenery: SHIP just stacks a board on the side table, with no bring-up test, LED, oven or tombstoning payoff (review 4's 'Bench + Oven' is still not built). So the success and failure moments for decoupling and heat are a toast, not an event. Adding a 2–3 s bring-up test (LED stutters or throttles for tier 1, steady for tier 2/3) would add both fun and teaching.
notes.playability: No soft-locks or console errors in either run (g.close() returned []). The full clean solve reached won with three boards shipped and 0 mistakes, and the A/A/A result card showed Pip in frame (qfn-teach-38). One hidden rule remains on board 3: layer-2 tracks must start on a via. In my first scripted run, a layer-2 GND track that started inside the exposed pad was refused because the EP vias weren't there yet. A player who draws on L2 first gets 'Start a layer 2 track on a via…', which explains it, and mid-stroke V helps, so review 4's item is partly fixed.
notes.models: Not my dimension. Incidental notes: the bench parts read cleanly at the bench camera. The QFN body's transparency plus the heat glow makes a pink wash over the exposed pad while dropping vias (qfn-teach-18).
